opus-5.5.text:
Developer feedback should shape it at almost every level. With most of the systems I've worked on, from Spark to the work we've done on compound AI systems, the biggest lessons came from watching what people actually tried to do, not from what we assumed they'd do.

I'd think about it in three layers.

**First, the interface.** Developers will tell you very quickly when an abstraction is fighting them. If people keep writing glue code around something or reaching for workarounds, that's a signal the API is at the wrong level. The goal is for the common case to be almost boring, while advanced users can still drop down and control the details.

**Second, failure modes.** The most valuable feedback is usually "here's where it broke on my data" or "here's where the output looked plausible but was wrong." Those cases are gold. You want to collect them systematically and turn them into evaluation sets, so you're not just fixing anecdotes but measuring whether each change actually helps across the board.

**Third, what to build next.** There's always a temptation to chase benchmarks or flashy demos. But if you listen closely, developers are usually asking for more mundane things: reliability, predictable cost and latency, better debugging, easier integration with their existing stack. Those unglamorous improvements often matter most for real adoption.

The meta-point is that the feedback loop itself is a product decision. You want to make it really easy for people to report issues, share examples, and see that their input changed something. When developers feel that, they become collaborators rather than just users, and that's when a project really takes off.

r001.rationale: It says to learn from what developers actually try to do and adjust abstractions when they force workarounds, connecting developer use cases to interface design.

r002.rationale: It describes a simple common case while letting advanced users control details, which communicates accommodating different preferences through customization.

r003.rationale: It mentions easier integration with developers’ existing stacks, but does not identify a compatibility layer across agents as Omnigen’s foundation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think developer feedback should be the thing that drives it, more than our own roadmap. Every project I've worked on that went well — Spark, MLflow, the agent work we've been doing at Databricks — got good because people took it, tried to do something we hadn't anticipated, and then told us exactly where it broke. That's the signal you can't get from inside a company.

With something like Omnigen, the risk is that you build toward an idealized workflow, the demo looks great, and then real developers have a messy codebase, a weird data format, a compliance requirement, and none of it fits. So I'd want a few things. First, a really tight loop on the rough edges: the error messages, the config that didn't make sense, the place where someone had to drop down and write glue code. Those small things compound, and they tell you where the abstraction is wrong.

Second, I'd pay attention to what people build on top of it rather than just what they ask for. When developers start wrapping a tool in their own layer, that's a sign the primitives are at the wrong level. You want to look at those wrappers and ask whether that should just be part of the product.

Third, and this is the one people get wrong, you have to be willing to say no. If you implement every request, you end up with something nobody can learn. The job is to take a thousand pieces of feedback, find the three underlying problems, and fix those. Often the best response to a feature request is making the thing someone was trying to do unnecessary.

And finally, be open about it. Public roadmaps, public issue trackers, shipping often enough that people see their feedback actually land. That's how you build the community that keeps giving you the honest signal in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says developers try unanticipated uses, and that feedback on wrappers and rough edges should reveal and correct abstractions.

r002.rationale: It discusses varied workflows and config problems, but does not say Omnigen should accommodate differing developer preferences through customization.

r003.rationale: It does not describe Omnigen as a compatibility layer across agents or identify that as its foundation.

astra-6.text:
I think developer feedback should be central, because the hard part is understanding where the system falls short in real applications. What are people trying to build? Where do they have to work around the model? And how do they decide whether a change is actually better?

I’d want a tight loop where developers can bring concrete examples of failures, we can turn those into evaluations, and then use those evaluations to guide improvements. You also want feedback on the whole experience—how easy it is to debug, how predictable the behavior is, and what the latency and cost look like. Those things can matter as much as the quality of an individual response.

r001.rationale: The response asks what developers are trying to build and says feedback should guide improvements, but it does not say that differing intended uses should shape Omnigen’s abstractions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses debugging, predictability, latency, and cost, but does not say developer tools should support different preferences through customization.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify a compatibility layer across agents as the foundation Omnigen aims to provide.

sol-6.1.text: I’d want to understand where developers are getting stuck in real workflows. What are they trying to build, what do they have to work around, and how do they know whether the result is good? That feedback should help us decide both what capabilities to improve and what interfaces to expose. Then you want a short iteration cycle: make a change, get it back into developers’ hands, and see whether it actually solves the problem.

r001.rationale: The response asks what developers are trying to build and says feedback should shape capabilities and interfaces, but it does not state that this feedback should guide the design of Omnigen’s abstractions.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention accommodating differing developer preferences through customization.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify a compatibility layer across agents as the foundation Omnigen aims to provide.
